en: Analysis of the Vibhaṅga:
The Analysis of the Analytical Knowledges (Paṭisambhidāvibhaṅga) – The Exposition According to the Discourses (Suttantabhājanīya)
1. The Chapter on Compendium:

The four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā)—the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhammapaṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of linguistic expression (niruttipaṭisambhidā), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā).

Knowledge regarding the meaning is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*); knowledge regarding the Dhamma is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*); knowledge regarding the expression of the terminology therein is the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*); and knowledge regarding knowledges is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*).
This is the section on inclusion. 2.
The Section on Truths (*Saccavāra*)
The four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā):

the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhammapaṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of linguistic expression (niruttipaṭisambhidā), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā).

Knowledge regarding suffering is the analytical knowledge of meaning; knowledge regarding the origin of suffering is the analytical knowledge of phenomena; knowledge regarding the cessation of suffering...

Knowledge of the meaning is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*); knowledge of the way leading to the cessation of suffering is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*);

knowledge regarding the expression of the terminology of those phenomena is the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*); and knowledge regarding knowledges is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*).
This is the section on the truths.
3. The Section on Causes (Hetuvāra):

The four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā)—the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhammapaṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of linguistic expression (niruttipaṭisambhidā), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā).

Knowledge regarding the cause is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhamma-paṭisambhidā*); knowledge regarding the fruit of the cause is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*attha-paṭisambhidā*); knowledge regarding the expression of the terminology for those phenomena is the analytical knowledge of language (*nirutti-paṭisambhidā*); and knowledge regarding these knowledges themselves is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*).
This is the section on causes. 4.
The Section on Phenomena (*Dhammavāra*).
There are four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā):

the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhammapaṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of linguistic expression (niruttipaṭisambhidā), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā).
Knowledge regarding those phenomena that have been born, become, produced, brought forth, and manifested—this is the analytical knowledge of meaning.

The knowledge regarding those phenomena from which those phenomena are born, become, produced, generated, fully manifested, and made apparent, is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhamma-paṭisambhidā*).

The knowledge regarding the verbal expression of the linguistic formulation therein is the analytical knowledge of language (*nirutti-paṭisambhidā*). The knowledge regarding knowledges is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā*).
This is the section on the Dhamma.
5. The Section on Dependent Origination:
The four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā).

The analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhammapaṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of linguistic expression (niruttipaṭisambhidā), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā).
Knowledge regarding aging and death is the analytical knowledge of meaning; knowledge regarding the origin of aging and death is the analytical knowledge of phenomena;

knowledge regarding the cessation of aging and death is the analytical knowledge of meaning; and knowledge regarding the practice leading to the cessation of aging and death is [the analytical knowledge of phenomena].

The analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā); therein, the knowledge regarding the expression of the terminology of phenomena is the analytical knowledge of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā);
the knowledge regarding knowledges is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā). These are the four analytical knowledges.
The analytical knowledge of meaning, the analytical knowledge of phenomena, the analytical knowledge of language, and the analytical knowledge of eloquence.
Knowledge regarding birth … [and so on] … knowledge regarding existence … [and so on].
Knowledge of clinging … knowledge of craving … knowledge of feeling … [and so on].
Knowledge of contact …pe… knowledge of the six sense bases …pe… knowledge of name-and-form …pe…

Knowledge regarding consciousness is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*); knowledge regarding volitional formations is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*); knowledge regarding the cessation of volitional formations is the analytical knowledge of meaning;
knowledge regarding the practice leading to the cessation of volitional formations is the analytical knowledge of phenomena.

In that regard, knowledge concerning the expression of the terminology of phenomena is the analytical knowledge of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā); knowledge concerning knowledges is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā).
This is the section on dependent origination.
6. The Section on the Discourses.
There are four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā):

the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhammapaṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of linguistic expression (niruttipaṭisambhidā), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā).
In this context, what is the analytical knowledge of phenomena?
Here, a bhikkhu knows the Dhamma—

the discourses (sutta), mixed prose and verse (geyya), expositions (veyyākaraṇa), verses (gāthā), inspired utterances (udāna), "thus-it-was-said" (itivuttaka), birth stories (jātaka), marvelous qualities (abbhutadhamma), and analytical expositions (vedalla).
This is called the "analytical knowledge of the Dhamma" (dhammapaṭisambhidā).
Thus he knows the meaning of each statement:
"This is the meaning of this statement; this is the meaning of that statement.

This is called the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*). In that regard, knowledge concerning the expression of the terminology of phenomena is the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*); knowledge concerning knowledges is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*).
This is the section on the textual tradition (pariyatti).
The Exposition of the Suttanta (suttantabhājanīya).
The Exposition of the Abhidhamma (abhidhammabhājanīya).
1. Section on the Wholesome (Kusalavāra) 1.1.
Sense-Sphere (Kāmāvacara) The four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā):

The analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*), the analytical knowledge of linguistic expression (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*).
What states are wholesome?

At whatever time a wholesome consciousness belonging to the sense sphere has arisen, accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, having a visible form as its object … [and so on] … pe … [as before].
Whether it be a mental object as its focal point or whatever else one has taken up, at that time there is contact … [and so on] … there is non-distraction.
These states are wholesome.
Knowledge regarding these states is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā).

Knowledge regarding their result is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*). Knowledge regarding the expression of the language by which those phenomena are designated is the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*).

The knowledge by which one knows those [other] knowledges—[thinking], "These knowledges illuminate this meaning"—is the knowledge regarding knowledges, the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*).
The four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā):

the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhammapaṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of linguistic expression (niruttipaṭisambhidā), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā).
What are the wholesome states (dhammā)?
At whatever time a wholesome sense-sphere consciousness has arisen that is accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, and with volitional effort … [and so on] … accompanied by joy,
dissociated from knowledge … [and so on] … accompanied by joy,
dissociated from knowledge, and with volitional effort … [and so on] …
Accompanied by equanimity and associated with knowledge … [and so on] … accompanied by equanimity,
associated with knowledge, and with volitional effort … [and so on] … accompanied by equanimity and dissociated from knowledge … [and so on].
Accompanied by equanimity, dissociated from knowledge, with volitional effort, having either a visible form as its object …pe… or mental phenomena as its object,
or whatever else it may be directed toward— at that time there is contact …pe… there is non-distraction.
These states are wholesome.
Knowledge regarding these phenomena is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā).
Knowledge regarding their result is the analytical knowledge of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā).
The knowledge regarding the expression of the linguistic formulation by which those phenomena are designated is the analytical knowledge of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā).

The knowledge by which one knows those various knowledges, thinking, "These knowledges illuminate this meaning"—this knowledge regarding knowledges is the analytical knowledge of ingenuity (paṭibhāna-patisambhidā). 1.2.
The Fine-Material Sphere (Rūpāvacara)
The four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā):

the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhammapaṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā), and the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā).
What are the wholesome states (kusalā dhammā)?

At whatever time one develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, secluded from sensual pleasures... [as before] ...and, having attained the first jhāna based on the earth-kasiṇa, dwells therein—at that time there is contact... [as before] ...there is non-distraction.
These states are wholesome.
Knowledge regarding these states is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā).
Knowledge regarding their result is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*).
Knowledge regarding the expression of the language by which those phenomena are designated is the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*).
The knowledge by which one knows those [other] knowledges is—
“The knowledge that ‘these knowledges illuminate this meaning’ is the analytical insight of perspicuity (paṭibhāna-patisambhidā) among knowledges.
1.3. Immaterial Sphere:
The four analytical insights (catasso paṭisambhidā).
The analytical knowledge of meaning, the analytical knowledge of phenomena, the analytical knowledge of language, and the analytical knowledge of eloquence.
What are wholesome states?
At whatever time one develops the path for rebirth in the formless realm, having completely transcended the base of nothingness—
Accompanied by the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, with the abandoning of pleasure … [as before] … he enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna;
at that time there is contact … [as before] … there is non-distraction.
These states are wholesome.
Knowledge regarding these phenomena is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhamma-paṭisambhidā*).
Knowledge regarding their result is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*attha-paṭisambhidā*).
The knowledge regarding the expression of the linguistic formulation by which those phenomena are designated is the analytical knowledge of language (*nirutti-paṭisambhidā*).

The knowledge by which one knows those various knowledges, thinking, "These knowledges illuminate this meaning"—this knowledge regarding knowledges is the analytical insight of ingenuity (*paṭibhāna-patisambhidā*). 1.4.
Supramundane.
The four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā):

the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhammapaṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā), and the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā).
What are wholesome states (kusalā dhammā)?
At whatever time one develops supramundane jhāna that leads to liberation, which results in the dismantling [of the substrata of existence],
for the abandoning of views and for the attainment of the first stage— being quite secluded from sensual pleasures … [as before] … one enters and dwells in the first jhāna,
which is difficult to practice and slow in direct knowledge— at that time there is contact … [as before] … there is non-distraction.
These states are wholesome.
Knowledge regarding these states is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā).
Knowledge regarding their result is the analytical knowledge of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā).

The knowledge regarding the expression of the language by which those phenomena are designated— that is, the knowledge concerning the verbal formulation of phenomena— is the analytical knowledge of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā).
The knowledge by which one knows those various knowledges,
thinking, "These knowledges illuminate this meaning"— that is, the knowledge regarding knowledges— is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā).
2. Section on the Unwholesome:

The four analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā)—the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhammapaṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā).
Which states are unwholesome?
At whatever time an unwholesome consciousness has arisen, accompanied by joy, associated with wrong view, having as its object a visible form …pe… or a mental phenomenon,
or whatever it may be upon which it is based— at that time there is contact …pe… there is non-distraction.
These phenomena are unwholesome.
Knowledge regarding these phenomena is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā).
Knowledge regarding their result is the analytical knowledge of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā).

The knowledge regarding the expression of the language by which those phenomena are designated— that is, the knowledge concerning the linguistic formulation of those phenomena— is the analytical knowledge of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā).
The knowledge by which one knows those knowledges themselves,
thinking, "These knowledges illuminate this meaning"— that is, the knowledge regarding knowledges— is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā).
The four analytical knowledges:
the analytical knowledge of meaning, the analytical knowledge of phenomena, the analytical knowledge of language, and the analytical knowledge of eloquence.
What are unwholesome states?
At whatever time an unwholesome state of consciousness has arisen that is accompanied by joy, associated with views,
and with volitional effort … [and so on] … accompanied by joy, dissociated from views … [and so on] … accompanied by joy, dissociated from views, and with volitional effort … [and so on].

Accompanied by equanimity and associated with views … [and so on] … accompanied by equanimity and associated with views with volitional effort … [and so on] … accompanied by equanimity and dissociated from views … [and so on].
Accompanied by equanimity, dissociated from views, with volitional effort … [and so on] … accompanied by grief,
associated with aversion … [and so on] … accompanied by grief,
associated with aversion, with volitional effort … [and so on].
Accompanied by equanimity and associated with doubt …pe… accompanied by equanimity and associated with restlessness, having visible form as its object …pe… or mental phenomena as its object,
or whatever else it may be directed toward— at that time there is contact …pe… there is non-distraction.
These phenomena are unwholesome.
Knowledge regarding these phenomena is the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhamma-paṭisambhidā).
Knowledge regarding their result is the analytical knowledge of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā).
The knowledge regarding the expression of the terminology for those phenomena by whatever language they are designated— that is the analytical knowledge of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā).
The knowledge by which one knows those various knowledges, thinking,
"These knowledges illuminate this meaning"— that knowledge regarding knowledges is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā).
3. Section on Ripening (Vipākavāra) 3.1.
Wholesome Ripening (Kusalavipāka) 3.1.1.
Rootless Wholesome (Ahetukakusala)
The three analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā):
the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhammapaṭisambhidā), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā).
Which phenomena are indeterminate (abyākata)?
At whatever time, as a result of having performed and accumulated wholesome karma pertaining to the sense sphere,
eye-consciousness arises accompanied by equanimity with a visible form as its object— at that time there is contact, there is feeling, there is perception,
there is volition, there is mind, there is equanimity, there is one-pointedness of mind, and there is the faculty of mind.
There is the equanimity faculty, there is the life faculty, or whatever other dependently arisen immaterial phenomena exist at that time.
These phenomena are indeterminate.
Knowledge regarding these phenomena is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*).
Knowledge regarding the verbal expression of the description of those phenomena, by whatever language their designation occurs, is the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*).
And the knowledge by which one knows those [other] knowledges—
“The knowledge that ‘these knowledges indicate this meaning’ is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā) among knowledges.
There are three analytical knowledges:
the analytical knowledge of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā), and the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā).”
Which phenomena are indeterminate?

At whatever time, as a result of having performed and accumulated wholesome kamma pertaining to the sense sphere, resultant ear-consciousness arises accompanied by equanimity with sound as its object; ... pe ...
resultant nose-consciousness arises accompanied by equanimity with odor as its object; ... pe ...
Tongue-consciousness arises accompanied by equanimity, having taste as its object ...
[and so on] ... body-consciousness arises accompanied by pleasure, having tangible objects as its object.
At that time there is contact, there is feeling, there is perception, there is volition, there is mind, there is pleasure, and there is one-pointedness of mind.
There is the mind faculty, there is the pleasure faculty, there is the life faculty,
or whatever other dependently arisen immaterial phenomena exist at that time.
These phenomena are indeterminate.
Knowledge regarding these phenomena is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*).
The knowledge regarding the expression of the language by which those phenomena are designated is the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*).
The knowledge by which one knows those [other] knowledges—
“The knowledge that ‘these knowledges illuminate this meaning’ is the analytical insight of perspicuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā) among knowledges.
There are three analytical insights:
the analytical insight of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā), the analytical insight of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā), and the analytical insight of perspicuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā).”
Which phenomena are indeterminate (*avyākata*)?

At whatever time, as a result of having performed and accumulated wholesome karma pertaining to the sense sphere, the resultant mind-element (*manodhātu*) arises accompanied by equanimity, having a visible form as its object, or ... pe ...
having a tangible object as its object, or whatever [object] it may be directed toward—at that time there is contact (*phassa*), there is feeling (*vedanā*).
There is perception, there is volition, there is consciousness, there is applied thought, there is sustained thought, there is equanimity,
there is one-pointedness of mind, there is the faculty of mind, there is the faculty of equanimity, there is the life-faculty, or whatever other dependent,
immaterial phenomena exist at that time.
These phenomena are indeterminate.
Knowledge regarding these phenomena is the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā).
The knowledge regarding the expression of the linguistic formulation by which those phenomena are designated is the analytical knowledge of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā).

The knowledge by which one knows those various knowledges, thinking, "These knowledges illuminate this meaning"—this knowledge regarding knowledges is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā). There are three analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā): [the analytical knowledge of dhamma, the analytical knowledge of meaning, and the analytical knowledge of perspicuity].

The analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*), the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*).
What are the indeterminate (*abyākata*) states?

At whatever time, as a result of having performed and accumulated wholesome karma belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), the resultant mind-consciousness element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) arises accompanied by joy, having a visible form as its object … [and so on] … pe … [up to] … having mental phenomena as its object.
Whether having mental phenomena as its object or whatever else it is directed toward, at that time there is contact, there is feeling, there is perception,
there is volition, there is consciousness, there is applied thought, there is sustained thought, there is rapture, there is pleasure,
there is one-pointedness of mind, there is the faculty of mind, there is the faculty of mental joy, and there is the life-faculty.
Or whatever other dependent-originated, immaterial phenomena exist at that time—
these phenomena are indeterminate.
Knowledge regarding these phenomena is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*).

The knowledge regarding the expression of the language by which those phenomena are designated— that is, the knowledge of the linguistic formulation of phenomena— is the analytical knowledge of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā).
The knowledge by which one knows those various knowledges,
thinking, “These knowledges illuminate this meaning”— that is, the knowledge regarding knowledges— is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā).
The three analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā):

the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhammapaṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of linguistic expression (niruttipaṭisambhidā), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā).
Which phenomena are indeterminate (abyākata)?
At whatever time, as a result of having performed and accumulated wholesome kamma pertaining to the sense sphere, the resultant mind-consciousness element arises accompanied by equanimity,
having either a visible form as its object …pe… or a mental phenomenon as its object, or whatever it may be directed toward— at that time there is contact,
there is feeling, there is perception, there is volition, there is consciousness, there is applied thought, there is sustained thought, there is equanimity, and there is one-pointedness of mind.
There is the mind faculty, there is the equanimity faculty, there is the life faculty,
or whatever other dependently arisen immaterial phenomena exist at that time.
These phenomena are indeterminate.
Knowledge regarding these phenomena is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*).
Knowledge regarding the expression of the language by which those phenomena are designated is the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*).
And the knowledge by which one knows those [other] knowledges—[this is the analytical knowledge of knowledge].
“The knowledge that ‘these knowledges illuminate this meaning’ is the analytical insight of eloquence (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā) among knowledges.
3.1.2. Sense-Sphere (Kāmāvacara):
Three Analytical Insights (Paṭisambhidā).

The analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*), the analytical knowledge of linguistic expression (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*).
What are the indeterminate (*abyākata*) states?

At whatever time, as a result of having performed and accumulated wholesome karma pertaining to the sense-sphere, the resultant mind-consciousness element arises accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge …pe…
Accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, with volitional effort … [and so on] … accompanied by joy,
dissociated from knowledge … [and so on] … accompanied by joy,
dissociated from knowledge, with volitional effort … [and so on].
Accompanied by equanimity and associated with knowledge … [and so on] … accompanied by equanimity and associated with knowledge,
with volitional effort … [and so on] … accompanied by equanimity and dissociated from knowledge … [and so on].

Accompanied by equanimity, dissociated from knowledge, with volitional effort, having either a visible form as its object …pe… or mental phenomena as its object, or whatever [object] it has taken up: at that time there is contact …pe… there is non-distraction.
These states are indeterminate (avyākata).
Knowledge regarding these phenomena is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*).
The knowledge regarding the expression of the language by which those phenomena are designated is the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*).
The knowledge by which one knows those [other] knowledges is—
“The knowledge that ‘these knowledges indicate this meaning’ is the analytical insight of eloquence (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā) among knowledges.
There are three analytical insights:
the analytical insight of meaning (attha-paṭisambhidā), the analytical insight of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā), and the analytical insight of eloquence (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā).”
Which phenomena are indeterminate (*avyākata*)?

At whatever time one develops the path for rebirth in the form realm, secluded from sensual pleasures... [as before] ...and, having attained the first absorption based on the earth-kasiṇa, dwells therein—at that time there is contact... [as before] ...there is non-distraction.
These phenomena are wholesome (*kusala*).
As a result of having performed and accumulated that very wholesome kamma pertaining to the fine-material sphere,
he— secluded from sensual pleasures … [as before] … enters and dwells in the first jhāna accompanied by the earth-kasiṇa; at that time there is contact … [as before] … there is non-distraction.
These phenomena are indeterminate.
Knowledge regarding these phenomena is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*attha-paṭisambhidā*).
The knowledge regarding the expression of the linguistic formulation by which those phenomena are designated is the analytical knowledge of language (*nirutti-paṭisambhidā*).

The knowledge by which one knows those various knowledges, thinking, "These knowledges illuminate this meaning"—this knowledge regarding knowledges is the analytical insight of ingenuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā). 3.1.3.
The Formless Realm (Arūpāvacara)
The three analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā):

the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhammapaṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of linguistic expression (niruttipaṭisambhidā), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā).
Which phenomena are indeterminate (abyākata)?
At whatever time one develops the path for rebirth in the formless realm, having completely transcended the base of nothingness,
and dwells having attained the fourth jhāna— accompanied by the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
with the abandoning of pleasure … [as before] … at that time there is contact … [as before] … there is non-distraction.
These states are wholesome.
Through the performance and accumulation of that very same wholesome karma of the formless realm, as its result, having completely transcended the base of nothingness,
accompanied by the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, with the abandoning of pleasure … [as before] … the fourth [jhāna].
When one enters and dwells in jhāna, at that time there is contact …pe… there is non-distraction.
These states are indeterminate.
Knowledge regarding these states is the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā).
The knowledge regarding the expression of the language by which those phenomena are designated— that is, the analytical knowledge of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā).
The knowledge by which one knows those various knowledges,
thinking, "These knowledges illuminate this meaning"— that is, the knowledge regarding knowledges, is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā).
3.1.4. Supramundane (Lokuttara) The three analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā):
the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā), and the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā).
Which phenomena are indeterminate?

At whatever time one develops supramundane jhāna that leads to liberation, conduces to the waning of existence, and results in the abandoning of wrong views, for the attainment of the first stage—secluded from sensual pleasures... [as before] ...one enters and dwells in the first jhāna.
At that time there is painful practice with sluggish direct knowledge; there is contact …pe… there is non-distraction.
These states are wholesome.
Through having performed and cultivated that very same supramundane wholesome karma, [one attains] the result, secluded from sensual pleasures.
... pe ... he enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is difficult to practice, slow in its direct knowledge, and empty.
At that time, there is contact ... pe ... there is non-distraction.
These phenomena are indeterminate (abyākata).
Knowledge regarding these phenomena is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*).
The knowledge regarding the expression of the linguistic formulation by which those phenomena are designated is the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*).
The knowledge by which one knows those [other] knowledges is—
“The knowledge that ‘these knowledges illuminate this meaning’ is the analytical insight of eloquence (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā) among knowledges.
3.2. Unwholesome Resultants:
Three analytical insights (tisso paṭisambhidā).

The analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dhammapaṭisambhidā*), the analytical knowledge of linguistic expression (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*), and the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*).
Which states are indeterminate (*abyākata*)?
At whatever time, as a result of having performed and accumulated unwholesome karma, eye-consciousness arises accompanied by equanimity with visible form as its object …pe… [and so on].
Ear-consciousness arises accompanied by equanimity, having sound as its object ...
nose-consciousness arises accompanied by equanimity, having odor as its object ...
tongue-consciousness arises accompanied by equanimity, having flavor as its object ... [and so on] ...
Body-consciousness arises accompanied by suffering, having tangible objects as its objective support. At that time, there is contact, there is feeling, there is perception,
there is volition, there is mind, there is suffering, there is one-pointedness of mind, there is the faculty of mind,
there is the faculty of suffering, there is the life-faculty, or whatever else [there may be] at that time.
At this time, there are also other immaterial phenomena that have arisen dependently.
These phenomena are indeterminate.
Knowledge regarding these phenomena is the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā).

The knowledge regarding the expression of the language by which those phenomena are designated— that is, the knowledge of the linguistic expression of phenomena— is the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*).
The knowledge by which one knows those various knowledges,
thinking, "These knowledges illuminate this specific meaning"— that is, the knowledge regarding knowledges— is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*).
The three analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā):
the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of phenomena (dhammapaṭisambhidā), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā).
Which phenomena are indeterminate (abyākata)?

At whatever time, as a result of having performed and accumulated unwholesome karma, the mind-element (*manodhātu*) arises accompanied by equanimity, having either a visible form as its object …pe… or a tangible object as its object …pe…;
or the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*) arises accompanied by equanimity, having either a visible form as its object …pe… [and so forth].
Whether having mental phenomena as its object or whatever else it is directed toward, at that time there is contact, there is feeling, there is perception,
there is volition, there is consciousness, there is applied thought, there is sustained thought, there is equanimity, there is one-pointedness of mind, there is the faculty of mind,
there is the faculty of equanimity, there is the life-faculty, or whatever other [states] there may be at that time.
At that time, there are also other immaterial phenomena that have arisen dependently.
These phenomena are indeterminate.
Knowledge regarding these phenomena is the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā).

The knowledge regarding the expression of the language by which those phenomena are designated— that is, the knowledge of the linguistic expression of phenomena— is the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*).
The knowledge by which one knows those [other] knowledges,
thinking, "These knowledges illuminate this meaning"— that is, the knowledge regarding knowledges— is the analytical knowledge of perspicuity (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*).
4. Section on Functioning (Kiriyavāra) Three analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā):
the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā), the analytical knowledge of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā).
Which phenomena are indeterminate (abyākata)?

At whatever time the mind-element (manodhātu) has arisen—being functional (kiriyā), neither wholesome nor unwholesome, and not the result of kamma—accompanied by equanimity (upekkhā), having visible form as its object, or ... pe ...
tangible objects as its object, or whatever else it may be directed toward—at that time there is contact (phassa), there is feeling (vedanā).
There is perception, there is volition, there is consciousness, there is applied thought, there is sustained thought, there is equanimity,
there is one-pointedness of mind, there is the faculty of mind, there is the faculty of equanimity, there is the life-faculty, or whatever other dependent,
immaterial phenomena exist at that time.
These phenomena are indeterminate.
Knowledge regarding these phenomena is the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā).
The knowledge regarding the expression of the linguistic formulation by which those phenomena are designated is the analytical knowledge of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā).
The knowledge by which one knows those various knowledges, thinking,
"These knowledges illuminate this meaning"— this knowledge regarding knowledges is the analytical insight of ingenuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā).
There are three analytical insights (paṭisambhidā).
The analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*), the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*), and the analytical knowledge of eloquence (*paṭibhānapaṭisambhidā*).
Which phenomena are indeterminate (*abyākata*)?

At whatever time the mind-consciousness element has arisen, which is functional (*kiriyā*), neither wholesome nor unwholesome, and not the result of kamma, accompanied by joy, and having a visible form as its object … [and so on] … [up to] … mental objects as its object.
Or with mental phenomena as object...

at that time the mind-consciousness element arises, which is functional, neither wholesome nor unwholesome, and not the result of kamma; it is accompanied by equanimity, and has either visible forms as its object...
or mental phenomena as its object, or whatever else it may be directed toward. At that time there is contact, there is feeling, there is perception.
There is contact, there is volition, there is consciousness, there is applied thought, there is sustained thought, there is equanimity,
there is one-pointedness of mind, there is the faculty of energy, there is the faculty of concentration, there is the faculty of mind, there is the faculty of equanimity,
there is the life-faculty, or whatever other dependent, immaterial phenomena exist at that time.
These phenomena are indeterminate.
Knowledge regarding these phenomena is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*).
The knowledge regarding the expression of the linguistic formulation by which those phenomena are designated is the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*).

The knowledge by which one knows those various knowledges, thinking, "These knowledges illuminate this meaning"—this knowledge regarding knowledges is the analytical insight of ingenuity (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā). There are three analytical insights (paṭisambhidā): [the analytical insight of dhamma, the analytical insight of meaning, and the analytical insight of ingenuity].
The analytical knowledge of meaning, the analytical knowledge of phenomena, the analytical knowledge of language, and the analytical knowledge of eloquence.
Which phenomena are indeterminate?

At whatever time the mind-consciousness element has arisen, which is functional (kiriyā), neither wholesome nor unwholesome, and not the result of kamma, accompanied by joy and associated with knowledge … [and so forth] … these are indeterminate phenomena.
Accompanied by joy, associated with knowledge, with volitional effort … [and so on] … accompanied by joy,
dissociated from knowledge … [and so on] … accompanied by joy,
dissociated from knowledge, with volitional effort … [and so on].
Accompanied by equanimity and associated with knowledge … [and so on] … accompanied by equanimity and associated with knowledge,
with volitional effort … [and so on] … accompanied by equanimity and dissociated from knowledge … [and so on].
Accompanied by equanimity, dissociated from knowledge, with volitional effort,

he develops a fine-material-sphere jhāna … pe … he develops an immaterial-sphere jhāna that is functional, neither wholesome nor unwholesome, not the result of kamma, a pleasant dwelling in this very life … pe …

Having completely transcended the base of nothingness, accompanied by the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, with the abandoning of pleasure … [as before] … one enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna; at that time there is contact … [as before] … there is non-distraction.
These states are indeterminate.
Knowledge regarding these phenomena is the analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*).
The knowledge regarding the expression of the language by which those phenomena are designated is the analytical knowledge of language (*niruttipaṭisambhidā*).
The knowledge by which one knows those [other] knowledges is—
“The knowledge that ‘these knowledges illuminate this meaning’ is the analytical insight of perspicuity (paṭibhāna-patisambhidā) among knowledges.
There are four analytical insights:

the analytical insight of meaning (attha-patisambhidā), the analytical insight of phenomena (dhamma-patisambhidā), the analytical insight of language (nirutti-patisambhidā), and the analytical insight of perspicuity (paṭibhāna-patisambhidā).”

The three analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) arise from the wholesome states of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara-kusala*) in the four types of consciousness associated with knowledge, and from the functional states (*kiriyā*) in the four types of consciousness associated with knowledge.
The analytical knowledge of meaning (*attha-paṭisambhidā*) arises in these same instances, and it also arises in the four paths and the four fruits.
This concludes the *Abhidhamma-bhājanīya*.
The Interrogation on Questions:
The four analytical knowledges—
the analytical knowledge of meaning, the analytical knowledge of phenomena, the analytical knowledge of language, and the analytical knowledge of eloquence.

Of the four analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*), how many are wholesome, how many unwholesome, and how many indeterminate? ... [and so on] ... how many are with conflict (*saraṇa*), and how many are without conflict (*araṇa*)?
1. The Triplet:
They may be wholesome, or they may be indeterminate.
They may be associated with pleasant feeling, or they may be associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
Three analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) may be states subject to result, or they may be states that are neither results nor subject to result;
the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) may be a result, or it may be a state subject to result, or it may be a state that is neither a result nor subject to result.
Three analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) are not-clung-to but subject to clinging;
the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) may be not-clung-to but subject to clinging, or it may be neither-clung-to nor subject to clinging.
Three analytical knowledges are undefiled and not subject to defilement.
The analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) may be undefiled yet subject to defilement, or it may be undefiled and not subject to defilement.
Three analytical knowledges are accompanied by both initial application and sustained application (savitakkasavicārā);

the analytical knowledge of meaning may be accompanied by both initial application and sustained application, or it may be without initial application and with sustained application only (avitakkavicāramattā), or it may be without both initial application and sustained application (avitakkaavicārā).
They may be accompanied by joy, they may be accompanied by pleasure, or they may be accompanied by equanimity.
They are not to be abandoned either by vision or by cultivation.
They do not have roots that are to be abandoned either by vision or by cultivation.
Three analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) may be conducive to accumulation, or they may be neither conducive to accumulation nor conducive to diminution.

The analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) may be conducive to accumulation, it may be conducive to diminution, or it may be neither conducive to accumulation nor conducive to diminution.

Three analytical knowledges are neither-learner-nor-non-learner (nevasekkhanāsekkha); the analytical knowledge of meaning may be a learner’s (sekkhā), it may be a non-learner’s (asekkhā), or it may be neither-learner-nor-non-learner.
Three analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) are limited;
the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) may be either limited or immeasurable.
The analytical knowledge of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā) has a limited object.
The three analytical knowledges may have limited objects, may have exalted objects, or may have immeasurable objects.
The three analytical knowledges are intermediate;
the analytical knowledge of meaning may be intermediate or sublime.
The three analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) are indeterminate.
The analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) may be either fixed in the rightness [of the path] or it may be indeterminate.
The analytical knowledge of language (niruttipaṭisambhidā) should not be described as having the path as its object, nor as having the path as its cause, nor as having the path as its predominance.

The analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) does not have the Path as its object; it may have the Path as its cause, it may have the Path as its dominant influence, or it may not be described as either "having the Path as its cause" or "having the Path as its dominant influence.

Two analytical knowledges may have the Path as their object, but do not have the Path as their cause; they may have the Path as their dominant influence, or they may not be described as either "having the Path as their object" or "having the Path as their dominant influence.
Three analytical knowledges may be arisen, may be unarisen, but are not to be described as "destined to arise."
The analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) may be arisen, may be unarisen, or may be bound to arise.
It may be past, future, or present.
The analytical knowledge of linguistic expression (niruttipaṭisambhidā) has the present as its object.
Two analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) may have the past as their object, may have the future as their object, or may have the present as their object.

The analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) may have the past as its object, may have the future as its object, may have the present as its object, or it may not be described as having the past as its object, nor the future as its object, nor the present as its object.
It may be internal, it may be external, or it may be both internal and external.
The analytical knowledge of language has an external object.
The other three analytical knowledges may have an internal object, may have an external object, or may have both an internal and external object.
They are non-demonstrable and non-reactive.
2. Duka 2.1.
Hetugocchaka (The Group on Roots) Roots;

accompanied by roots; associated with roots; both roots and accompanied by roots; both roots and associated with roots; they should not be called "neither root nor accompanied by roots," nor should they be called "not-root and not-accompanied-by-root."
2.2. The Minor Intermediate Dyads With conditions;

conditioned; non-demonstrable; non-reacting; immaterial; three analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) are mundane; the analytical knowledge of meaning may be mundane or supramundane; cognizable by some, not cognizable by others.
2.3. The Group on the Taints (āsava)
There are no taints.
The three analytical knowledges are with taints;
the analytical knowledge of meaning may be with taints or without taints.
They are dissociated from the taints (*āsava*).
The three analytical knowledges (*paṭisambhidā*) should not be said to be "both taints and associated with taints," but rather they are "associated with taints and not themselves taints.

The analytical knowledge of meaning (*atthapaṭisambhidā*) should not be said to be "both a taint and associated with taints"; it may be "associated with taints and not itself a taint," or it may not be said to be "associated with taints and not itself a taint."
They should not be described as "both taints and associated with taints," nor as "associated with taints but not taints.
The three analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) are dissociated from taints and are with-taint (sāsava).
The analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) may be dissociated from taints and with-taint, or it may be dissociated from taints and without-taint (anāsava).
2.4. The Group of Fetters, etc.
They are not fetters … [and so on] … they are not ties … [and so on] …
There are no floods … [and so on] … there are no yokes … [and so on] … there are no hindrances … [and so on] …
No misapprehensions ... [etc.
... 2.10. The Greater Pair:
With an object.
They are not mind, not mental factors, not associated with mind, not conjoined with mind, not produced by mind, not co-existent with mind, and do not follow after the mind.

They are conjoined with and produced by mind, co-existent with what is conjoined with and produced by mind, and follow after what is conjoined with and produced by mind; they are external, not derived, and not clung-to.
2.11. The Group on Clinging (Upādāna-gocchaka), etc.
There are no clingings … [and so on] … no defilements … [and so on] … they are not to be abandoned by vision.
Not to be abandoned by cultivation.
Not having as their cause that which is to be abandoned by vision.
Not having as their cause that which is to be abandoned by cultivation.
Three analytical knowledges are accompanied by applied thought;
the analytical knowledge of meaning may be accompanied by applied thought, or it may be without applied thought.
Three analytical knowledges are accompanied by sustained thought.
The analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) may be accompanied by sustained thought (savicārā), or it may be without sustained thought (avicārā).
It may be accompanied by rapture (sappītikā), or it may be without rapture (appītikā).
It may be associated with rapture (pītisahagatā), or it may not be associated with rapture (na pītisahagatā).
They may be accompanied by pleasure, or they may not be accompanied by pleasure.
They may be accompanied by equanimity, or they may not be accompanied by equanimity.
The three analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) belong to the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara).
The analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) may be of the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), or it may not be of the sense sphere.
It is not of the fine-material sphere (rūpāvacara).
It is not of the immaterial sphere (arūpāvacara).
Three analytical knowledges are included within the mundane;
the analytical knowledge of meaning may be either mundane or supramundane.
Three analytical knowledges do not lead to liberation.
The analytical knowledge of meaning may be leading to liberation, or it may not be leading to liberation.
The other three analytical knowledges are indeterminate;
the analytical knowledge of meaning may be determinate, or it may be indeterminate.
The three analytical knowledges (paṭisambhidā) are surpassable;
the analytical knowledge of meaning (atthapaṭisambhidā) may be surpassable or it may be unsurpassable.
This is called "without conflict" (araṇa).
The Section on Questioning.
The Analysis of the Analytical Knowledges is finished.
